items.abstract: <jats:p>The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a de facto standard for integrating Large Language Models with external tools, yet no formal security analysis of the protocol specification exists. We present the first rigorous security analysis of MCP's architectural design, identifying three fundamental protocol-level vulnerabilities: (1) absence of capability attestation allowing servers to claim arbitrary permissions, (2) bidirectional sampling without origin authentication enabling server-side prompt injection, and (3) implicit trust propagation in multi-server configurations. We implement MCPBench, a novel framework bridging existing agent security benchmarks to MCP-compliant infrastructure, enabling direct measurement of protocol-specific attack surfaces. Through controlled experiments on 847 attack scenarios across five MCP server implementations, we demonstrate that MCP's architectural choices amplify attack success rates by 23--41% compared to equivalent non-MCP integrations. We propose MCPSec, a backward-compatible protocol extension adding capability attestation and message authentication, reducing attack success rates from 52.8% to 12.4% with median latency overhead of 8.3ms per message. Our findings establish that MCP's security weaknesses are architectural rather than implementation-specific, requiring protocol-level remediation.</jats:p>
title: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification and Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents

                  <jats:p>Протокол Model Context Protocol (MCP) стал де-факто стандартом для интеграции больших языковых моделей с внешними инструментами, однако официального анализа безопасности спецификации протокола не существует. Мы представляем первый тщательный анализ безопасности архитектурного дизайна MCP, в котором выявлены три фундаментальные уязвимости на уровне протокола: (1) отсутствие подтверждения возможностей, позволяющее серверам запрашивать произвольные разрешения, (2) двунаправленная выборка без аутентификации источника, позволяющая вводить запросы со стороны сервера, и (3) неявная передача доверия в конфигурациях с несколькими серверами. Мы реализуем ProtoAmp, новую платформу, соединяющую существующие тесты безопасности агентов с инфраструктурой, совместимой с MCP, что позволяет напрямую измерять поверхности атаки, специфичные для протокола. items.abstract: The world is running out of the old internet addresses (IPv4). The new system, called IPv6, was created to solve this problem. Many people talk about the theory of IPv6, but this paper focuses on how it actually works in practice. We built simple computer programs to explore IPv6. One program checks and explains what an IPv6 address means. Another program searches for active devices on an IPv6 network. A third program watches the raw data sent over the network to show how IPv6 devices talk to each other. By using these tools, we make the concepts of IPv6 easy to see and understand. This hands on approach helps show the real benefits and challenges of IPv6, proving that practical experience is key to building the next generation of the internet.
title: Empirical Analysis of IPv6 Protocol Implementation: A Comprehensive Framework for Address Validation, Network Discovery, and Security Assessment

items.abstract: <jats:p>As large language models transition from conversational assistants to autonomous agents capable of executing actions inside enterprise infrastructure, the primary security risk shifts from model hallucination to ungoverned delegation of execution authority to probabilistic systems. A fundamental architectural question emerges: how should execution authority be governed when the decision-making component is nondeterministic? This paper proposes protocol-mediated execution layers as a governance architecture for LLM agent systems. Rather than relying on prompt-based behavioral suggestions, which are probabilistic, bypassable, and unenforceable, we argue that execution governance must be implemented as structural infrastructure external to the model. We present a concrete architecture in which the LLM functions as a reasoning engine that expresses intent, while a protocol layer (instantiated here as Model Context Protocol infrastructure) enforces authorization, validates inputs against formal schemas, constrains execution to pre-defined capability boundaries, and maintains an immutable audit trail. Drawing on Zero Trust principles [13] and foundational work in capability-based security [12, 16], we establish direct architectural parallels to operating system kernels, API gateways, and container orchestration control planes, demonstrating that every generation of computing has solved the same governance problem through the same fundamental pattern. We present a production implementation, NovoMCP, a drug discovery platform managing 122 million molecular records, as an empirical case study demonstrating four governance layers: schemabased tool definitions, tiered access control, pre-execution resource accounting, and service-level isolation. We further identify an underexplored dimension of the governance problem: input-side control. While most discussions focus on constraining model outputs (what the agent can do), we argue that a complete governance envelope must also constrain model inputs (what context, tools, and data sources the agent can access). We propose admissibility gates and behavioral drift detection as complementary mechanisms, and identify drift detection across sequences of individually authorized actions as a key open problem. 1 The central thesis is a reframe: the question is not whether to trust AI agents, but what architectural controls make them trustworthy. The answer, consistent with five decades of computing history, is: trust the protocol, not the process.</jats:p>
title: Protocol-Mediated Execution Governance for LLM Agent Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on multi-step reasoning and analogical transfer (often across domains), yet current practices often lack explicit governance, auditability, and structured verification. This paper introduces the Structural Alignment and Verification Protocol (SAVP), a protocollevel governance framework that decomposes reasoning into four inspectable stages: structure extraction, alignment proposal, solution synthesis, and verification. SAVP emphasizes explicit intermediate artifacts-alignment mappings and verification traces-that enable structured auditing, ablation, and reproducible evaluation. Prompt examples are illustrative only; the contribution is the protocol and auditable artifacts. SAVP is positioned as an auditable verification layer for LLM reasoning systems, situated at the intersection of artificial intelligence methodology and evaluation design. While motivated by analogical reasoning, the protocol generalises to broader structured reasoning and verification scenarios. This staged release focuses on protocol specification, trace schema design, and an evaluation blueprint, including the Distal Analogy Suite (DAS) for controlled distal cross-domain testing. Prompt examples and pilot traces are provided solely as illustrative realizations of the protocol and should not be interpreted as normative prompting recipes. The current version does not claim empirical performance improvements; full benchmarking and large-scale ablations are reserved for subsequent revisions. This paper provides a protocol specification and pilot results to validate the artifact pipeline, with full benchmarking deferred. This paper argues that treating reasoning workflows as protocol-governed processes-with explicit verification artifacts-offers a practical pathway toward more transparent and auditable LLM reasoning research.</jats:p>
title: From Structural Alignment to Verification Governance: A Protocol for Auditable LLM Reasoning Protocol Specification and Evaluation Blueprint

items.abstract: As multi-agent AI systems scale to production, the protocols connecting them constrain their capabilities. Current protocols such as Google's A2A and Anthropic's MCP omit model-level metadata, preventing quality-aware routing, efficient communication, and governance. We present the LLM Delegate Protocol (LDP), which introduces five AI-native primitives: rich delegate identity cards, progressive payload negotiation, governed sessions, structured provenance, and trust domains. We implement LDP as a plugin adapter for the JamJet agent runtime and evaluate it against A2A and random baselines. Identity-aware routing achieves 12x lower latency on easy tasks; semantic frame payloads reduce token count by 37 percent with no quality loss; governed sessions eliminate 39 percent token overhead; and noisy provenance degrades quality below the no-provenance baseline, showing that confidence metadata is harmful without verification. Trust domain and fallback analyses demonstrate architectural advantages in security and resilience. This paper contributes a protocol design, reference implementation, and initial evidence that AI-native protocol primitives enable more efficient and governable multi-agent delegation.
title: LDP: An Identity-Aware Protocol for Multi-Agent LLM Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>The advent of Industry 4.0 has made people pay more and more attention to the security of the industrial control system. As a common and typical communication protocol, Modbus does not consider the problem of data security at the beginning of its design, which provides opportunities for criminals. In this paper, we design a security scheme to protect the traditional Modbus TCP protocol, by using domestic encryption algorithms. As a result, the proposed scheme is able to identity authentication, data encryption, data integrity check, and anti-replay attacks. Security analysis and experimental results show that our proposed scheme solves the security problem of Modbus TCP protocol with minimal overhead increase.</jats:p>
title: Design and Implementation of a Lightweight Security-Enhanced Scheme for Modbus TCP Protocol

items.abstract: <jats:p>Human-AI collaboration challenges persist even when AI systems are technically capable. We argue these challenges may often stem from Silent Intent Inferencea structural pattern where AI resolves semantic ambiguity without explicit user authorization. We propose framing this not as mere interaction friction but as a potential accountability challenge: it may create oversight gaps, dicult-to-trace decisions, and gradual reduction of user agency. We introduce the Collaboration Protocol (CP), a theoretical framework for preserving human semantic authority through four operationalized constructs: (1) Intent Control Degree (ICD), a user-adjustable parameter (0.01.0) governing how ambiguity is resolved; (2) Intent Pivot Points (IPP), semantic locations where meaning may branch, with a six-type taxonomy; (3) Intent Fidelity Index (IFI), a composite metric measuring intent preservation across interactions; and (4) Context Roots (CR), a mechanism for anchoring ambiguity in interaction history, enabling multi-turn and multi-session intent tracking. The framework introduces the Semantic Materiality Proxy (SMP) for objective ambiguity classication and the Context Factor (CF) for modeling how prior interactions aect current ambiguity. Each construct includes specic measurement procedures enabling empirical validation. We propose a phased research agenda: quantifying silent inference prevalence in current LLM systems, validating ICD eects on collaboration quality, and establishing IPP annotation reliability. This paper establishes a falsiable theoretical foundationthe constructs and hypotheses are designed to be empirically tested and potentially refuted by the research community.</jats:p>
title: The Collaboration Protocol: Silent Intent Inference as an Accountability Challenge in Human-LLM Interaction

items.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence and machine learning continue to advance, we must understand their strategic importance in national security. This paper focuses on unique AI applications in the military, emphasizes strategic imperatives for success, and aims to rekindle excitement about AI's role in national security. We will examine the United States progress in integrating AI into the battle space, discuss the importance of securing these technologies from adversaries, and explore the challenges and risks associated with their integration. Finally, we will highlight the strategic significance of AI to national security and a set of strategic imperatives for military leaders and policymakers.</jats:p>
title: Optimizing National Security Strategies through LLM-Driven Artificial Intelligence Integration

items.abstract: <jats:p><p>This paper delves into the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) as they pertain to national security, with a particular emphasis on their integration into military applications. Through an in-depth analysis of the United States' progress in assimilating AI technologies into the battle space, the paper seeks to reinvigorate enthusiasm about the potential of AI in safeguarding national interests. Key aspects of this paper include the necessity of protecting AI systems from adversaries, as well as the inherent challenges and risks that come with integrating them into military operations. The paper concludes by underscoring the strategic significance of AI in the realm of national security and outlines a set of strategic imperatives for military leaders and policymakers to ensure success in this critical domain.</p></jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Adversarial attacks pose an important threat to the security and trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs). These models are vulnerable to carefully engineered input designed to exploit their weaknesses, degrade system performance, and extract private information. Practical countermeasures need a strong offensive strategy that includes adversarial scenarios simulation to test how models hold up in various conditions. Adversarial data poisoning and evasion techniques are particularly useful as they can reveal strengths during training and inference processes, respectively. Through systematic identification and mitigation of every vulnerability, organizations can strengthen the model's robustness to real-world attacks. This technical framework also emphasizes the need to embed adversarial simulations into the security cycle of LLMs to prevent risks associated with malicious actors. Via iterative analysis, an organization can increase the robustness of a model and build a resilient infrastructure for secure implementation of LLMs in sensitive/high-level environments.</jats:p>
title: LLM Security and Guardrail Defense Techniques in Web Applications

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of large language models (LLMs) into mobile applications introduces new vectors for security and privacy vulnerabilities. This study proposes an automated framework for systematically testing LLM-enabled mobile apps, focusing on identifying potential threats such as prompt injection, data leakage, unauthorized access, and adversarial manipulation. The approach combines dynamic analysis, static code inspection, and machine learning-based anomaly detection to evaluate app behaviors in real-time. Our method ensures scalability and efficiency across diverse mobile platforms and LLM configurations. Results demonstrate significant improvements in detection rates and response times compared to conventional manual testing. This work aims to bridge the gap between AI innovation and secure mobile deployment, promoting trust in AI-integrated ecosystems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Time Sensitive Networking (TSN) will be an integral component of industrial networking. Time synchronization in TSN is provided by the IEEE-1588, Precision Time Protocol (PTP) protocol. The standard, dating back to 2008, marginally addresses security aspects, notably not encompassing the frames designed for management purposes (Type Length Values or TLVs). In this work we show that the TLVs can be abused by an attacker to reconfigure, manipulate, or shut down time synchronization. The effects of such an attack can be serious, ranging from interruption of operations to actual unintended behavior of industrial devices, possibly resulting in physical damages or even harm to operators. The paper analyzes the root causes of this vulnerability, and provides concrete examples of attacks leveraging it to de-synchronize the clocks, showing that they can succeed with limited resources, realistically available to a malicious actor.</jats:p>
title: Time sensitive networking security: issues of precision time protocol and its implementation

items.abstract: The traditional JTAG debugging interface lacks built-in security mechanisms, rendering it vulnerable to attacks such as data theft and code injection, which poses a serious threat in critical security scenarios, including the Internet of Things and embedded systems. Existing security enhancement schemes, such as static key authentication and public key cryptographic protocols, generally face problems like complex key management, high computational overhead, or poor scene adaptability, making it difficult to achieve secure, efficient, and flexible debugging protection in resource-constrained environments.To address these challenges, this paper proposes a JTAG security debugging architecture based on a configurable protocol stack. The core contributions are: (1) A hierarchical, policy-driven security protocol framework enabling dynamic adaptation of authentication strength and debugging permissions; (2) A lightweight authentication mechanism achieved by reconfiguring the internal lookup tables and round constants of the SHA-1 algorithm, reducing bus information leakage while maintaining minimal hardware overhead; (3) Dynamic session key-based encryption combined with stream ciphering to ensure per-session confidentiality, effectively implementing a “one-time-per-session” security model.The architecture was implemented and validated on the Xilinx VU-19P FPGA platform. Experimental results demonstrate that the system effectively mitigates replay and eavesdropping attacks, with only marginal increases in logic resource usage and latency. It further supports adaptive security policy adjustments based on debugging phase and target access rights. Compared to existing approaches, this work achieves a superior balance among security, flexibility, and resource efficiency, offering a scalable hardware implementation for JTAG security in resource-constrained devices.
title: Architecture Design and Implementation of a Custom Protocol-Based JTAG Debugging Protection System for Enhanced Hardware Security

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models consistently underperform as specialized advisors due to context drift, personality inconsistency, and inability to prioritize curated knowledge sources. This paper introduces the Operational Protocol Method, a systematic approach for LLM specialization and assistance through structured persona engineering and collaborative development processes. The method transforms generic LLMs into reliable subject matter expert advisors while enabling coordinated multi-agent systems that maintain expertise boundaries across complex advisory tasks. Case studies in personal finance and note-taking demonstrate the method's practical effectiveness and versatility across domains.</jats:p>
title: The Operational Protocol Method: Systematic LLM Specialization Through Collaborative Persona Engineering and Agent Coordination

items.abstract: <jats:p>Methods for the early warning of cascading failures in large language model (LLM) agent systems currently report "early detection" in mutually incompatible units: the fraction of the execution log consumed before an alarm, the number of interaction rounds before a semantic violation on synthetic data, the number of turns after an attack has been injected, or the number of turns before a safety violation. These quantities measure different things and cannot be compared. As a consequence, the field cannot answer the two questions that matter to an operator: how much time remains to react, and how many false alarms will be raised on normal traffic. We propose PrefixBench, an open evaluation protocol and harness under which early-warning methods become comparable. A monitor observes only the prefix of a trajectory, and lead time is measured to one of four explicitly annotated endpoints: first error, propagation onset, explicit violation, and terminal failure. The protocol fixes six jointly reported metrics-coverage, lead time, premature alarm rate, benign false alarm rate with alarm burden, actionable margin, and intervention net benefit-and requires that methods be compared at a matched benign false-alarm budget rather than by a single AUROC value. We contribute the protocol definitions, a harness architecture that structurally prevents label and future-event leakage, a data and annotation design that combines fault injection, re-annotation of public trajectories and benign runs, and a pre-specified experimental plan with six experiments. Our central hypothesis is that, once the endpoint, the prefix-only regime and the operator-facing metrics are fixed, the ranking of existing methods will change, and part of the reported lead time will prove to be an artefact of annotation or post-hoc scoring. This paper is primarily a protocol and benchmark-design proposal. As a pilot, we run the harness on the test split of AFTraj-2K with two trivial baselines: at benign false-alarm budgets of up to 10%, they warn before the first error on at most 3.7% of failing trajectories, and reporting any alarm in the trace instead of the first alarm inflates coverage by a factor of two to four.</jats:p>
title: PrefixBench: An Evaluation Protocol for Early Warning of Cascading Failures in LLM Agent Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p><span>The limitation in current human-LLM interaction: users offer under-specified inputs, while the model compensates for missing information provided by substituting statistical correlations. Causal Override, a machine produces outputs that are fluent but misaligned with user intent systematically, which results in Intent Decay where compound errors accumulate across multi-agent workflows. We propose Fathom-then-Generate (FtG), which is a reversible protocol for intent alignment that is used&nbsp; to optimize the input side of LLM interaction. FtG uses the user’s knowledge as an information source to build a mental model that must be structured and verified systematically before the generation process happens. Referring to the communication model of Lasswell (1948), the 5W1H (WHY, WHAT, WHO, WHEN, WHERE, HOW) coordinate system indicates the completeness of information. Fathom Depth, a computable metric formed on the basis of Shannon's (1948) information entropy, determines when sufficient understanding has been achieved. The system constructs an Intent Graph—a directed knowledge graph with not just factual information but also beliefs, assumptions, emotions, values, and causal reasoning, where every edge has provenance metadata which tells us if the information was stated by the user or system-inferred from the context. Intent Transparency, the system’s representation of user intent is at all stages visible, auditable, and reversible by the user. Conversely, in current agent architectures, the reasoning chains are not accessible to or auditable by the user. Within FtG, the Causal Fathom Protocol (CFP) defines how human causal reasoning is extracted, marked, verified, and transmitted to downstream models as hard constraints that inhibit the Causality Override to succeeding models. A deterministic compiler transforms the fathomed Intent Graph into a structured prompt. The model generates once, from complete information, rather than iterating on incomplete inputs. FtG requires no model fine-tuning, no access to model internals, and operates with any downstream LLM through standard API calls.</span></jats:p>
title: Fathom-then-Generate: A Reversible Intent Alignment Protocol for Human-LLM Interaction with Causal Fidelity

items.abstract:
<jats:p>The prevailing literature suggests that large language model (LLM) systems remain vulnerable to prompt injection and other adversarial inputs, while existing LLM-based defenses do not provide deterministic assurance against such attacks. This paper therefore treats the LLM as insecure.It follows that a mechanism intended to secure an LLM must itself be independent of LLM technology. For sufficiently bounded domains, this paper proposes a deterministic front end that permits only validated, structured representations of user requests to cross a trust boundary protecting the LLM and security-critical information. The front end neither requires nor assumes an LLM; what consumes its output is irrelevant to its operation. 
<div>
 The paper further proposes that this front end can take the form of a deterministic natural-language interface (NLI), preserving the flexibility of an LLM-style prompt interface. Rather than attempting to anticipate all possible expressions, the NLI can be developed from a corpus of actual domain interactions using techniques derived from pre-LLM speech recognition and natural-language processing. The resulting classifier deterministically maps recognized input to permitted structured representations and rejects ambiguous, incomplete, or out-of-domain input.
</div>
<div>
 If sufficiently comprehensive, such an NLI may, at least for ordinary legitimate queries, be functionally indistinguishable to the user from a domainrestricted probabilistic LLM interface, while ensuring that unvalidated user input never crosses the trust boundary
</div></jats:p>
title: Securing Bounded-Domain LLM Systems Using Deterministic Natural-Language Security Gateways

items.abstract: <jats:p>Traders increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to turn a strategy described in desk language into executable code. We measure the cost of that translation. Holding the strategy, the price path and the frictions fixed, we compare a reference implementation with the implementation an LLM writes from the same description; the return difference is an implementation shortfall attributable to translation alone, with the strategy’s own alpha differenced away. Across equity index and cryptocurrency markets, most programs written by low-cost models run without error yet depart from the authorised behaviour, and the median absolute shortfall ranges from several hundred to over two thousand basis points of initial equity. The sign of the average shortfall varies across models and samples, so the loss is better described as unpredictable deviation than as a haircut. The shortfall is larger for strategies whose risk logic carries state for longer, but this gradient is explained by holding duration: within a given type of risk control, models do not diverge more often on longer-state logic, and each divergence costs more the longer the strategy stays in position. We find no robust evidence that volatility amplifies the loss, and errors are close to independent across strategies, so the risk is largely diversifiable. Frontier models still diverge silently on more than a quarter of tasks, and neither compilation, backtesting nor an LLM code review detects the divergence.</jats:p>
title: Silent Implementation Shortfall in LLM-Written Trading Code

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for primary title and abstract screening in evidence synthesis. Autonomous use, meaning an LLM that issues EXCLUDE decisions without human confirmation, depends on very high recall. Within a planned evidencesynthesis workstream whose eligibility rubric spans eight evidence families centred on clinicalguideline updating and recommendation evolution, this study specified, in dated and internally hash-locked protocol documents (prospectively specified internal documentation; this study was not publicly preregistered), a validation requirement for permitting autonomous AI screening: the exact one-sided 95% lower confidence bound on the LLM’s recall for relevant records, measured against a human dual-reviewer reference standard, had to reach 95%. Objective. To determine whether one specific LLM screening configuration, frozen before Gate C execution as recorded in dated internal documentation, met this protocol-defined recall requirement on the study’s calibration frame. Methods. The evaluation used a 1,048-record stratified, relevance-enriched calibration frame, which was not a representative sample of the larger sealed search corpus of approximately 4,082 records (about 61% of the frame was an entire citation-chained methods-literature stratum, plus fixed clinical [n = 200] and legislative [n = 150] proxy draws and a fixed 60-record difficultnegative stress set). Two reviewers independently classified every frame record (INCLUDE / EXCLUDE / UNRESOLVED) against the study rubric; decision sets were hash-locked before comparison; disagreements were reconciled by documented discussion, with an unresolved disagreement recorded as UNRESOLVED (not defaulted to INCLUDE) and referred to a third reviewer. One of the two initial reviewers was the study author, so the reference standard is not fully independent of the study team. A verbatim, hash-locked prompt was then run once over the entire frame in 43 batches through the Claude Code Agent tool, a subscription-based agent interface (requested model parameter value “sonnet”; the retained execution record identifies this invocation surface but carries no independently checkable model-identity string beyond that label). Model outputs were joined to the sealed reference standard by identifier; the single UNRESOLVED record was excluded from binary denominators and reported separately. The primary outcome was recall (reference-INCLUDE records the model called INCLUDE or UNCERTAIN, both of which route to human review under the design, divided by all reference-INCLUDE records), with an exact one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound and a protocol-defined two-outcome rule (a lower bound of 95% or above meets the requirement; below 95% does not). The one-sided Clopper–Pearson lower bound was the protocol-defined decision statistic for this relevance-enriched frame and is not a confidence bound for recall in the parent corpus or in any other corpus. Specificity, falsepositive rate, raw agreement, the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), the lost-evidence quantity (reference-INCLUDE records routed to model EXCLUDE), and family-level results are descriptive secondary outcomes and are properties of this relevance-enriched frame, not corpuswide estimates. Results. Model output covered all 1,048 records (1,048 unique identifiers; no duplicates or omissions). The reference standard contained 498 INCLUDE, 549 EXCLUDE, and 1 UNRESOLVED record; pre-reconciliation reviewer agreement was 76.5% (Cohen’s kappa 0.55). Of 498 confirmedrelevant records in the frame, the frozen configuration preserved 234 for human review and routed 264 to EXCLUDE. Observed recall was 46.99% (234/498); the exact one-sided 95% Clopper– Pearson lower bound was 43.23%, against the protocol-defined 95% requirement. The requirement was not met, and this is a permanent result for this calibration run under the study’s governance rules. On this frame, 264 of 498 reference-relevant records (53.01%) were routed to model EXCLUDE (lost evidence; the complement of recall). Descriptive secondary metrics on this frame were specificity 83.42%, false-positive rate 16.58%, raw agreement 66.09%, and MCC 0.3283. Missed relevant records were concentrated: 181 of 264 (68.6%) were in one evidence family (clinical-guideline updating, implementation, comparison, and versioning), and 244 of 264 (92.4%) in that family plus the information-retrieval family. For the entity-resolution and record-linkage family, observed frame-level recall was 96.40%, with a one-sided 95% lower bound of 92.59%. A protocol-specified diagnostic analysis, conducted after the gate outcome was determined and introducing no new data, suggested that many exclusions were consistent with the narrower operational construct specified in the frozen prompt.&nbsp;</jats:p>
title: Evaluating a Frozen LLM Configuration for Clinical-Guideline Literature Screening: A Protocol-Defined Validation Study

<jats:p><p>The rapid enterprise deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agentic AI systems has outpaced the security practices required to operate them safely. Traditional penetration testing methodologies — built on deterministic system assumptions — fail to address the probabilistic, natural-language attack surface introduced by AI deployments. This paper presents a structured, five-phase practitioner framework for LLM and agentic AI security testing, grounded in documented real-world attack patterns and aligned to OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025), OWASP Agentic Top 10 (2026), and MITRE ATLAS v5.1.0. The framework addresses four critical attack classes — indirect prompt injection via RAG corpus poisoning, agentic goal hijacking through multi-turn social engineering, system prompt leakage, and MCP tool poisoning — providing exploitation methodology, detection engineering guidance, and MITRE ATLAS technique mappings for each. Defensive countermeasures are presented across prevention, detection, and response layers, including sample detection logic for integration into SIEM and CI/CD pipelines. The paper establishes that organizations deploying AI systems without AI-specific security testing face material risks of data exfiltration, unauthorized autonomous action, and regulatory violation — and that a structured methodology mapped to existing frameworks is sufficient to close the execution gap.</p>
<p></p></jats:p>
title: Breaking AI: A Practitioner's Framework for LLM and Agentic AI Security Testing

items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 When a pipeline's output carries legal weight, a verifier that reads an implementer's claims and reasons about them produces an opinion. What a compliance record requires is primary execution evidence produced independently of those claims. This paper presents a dual-agent coordination protocol in which the verifying agent re-executes the production pipeline directly, before reading the implementing agent's self-verification results, and posts its findings as first-hand evidence with file-and-line citations to the live codebase. We call this ratification to distinguish it from review, critique, scoring, and debate. Ratification is the act of confirming a claim through independent re-execution of the system the claim describes, not through reasoning about the claim itself.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;The protocol is mediated by two directional append-only outbox files on a shared filesystem. Each file has exactly one writer. A filesystem watcher fires on each file when new content is appended, waking the opposing agent without polling. Neither agent can modify what the other has written. Retraction is public, timestamped, and permanent. The outbox files serve simultaneously as coordination channel, audit trail, and session memory across sessions measured in days.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; We demonstrate the protocol in a multi-week production session on a candidate screening system operating under EU AI Act Article 9 risk management, Article 13 transparency, and Article 15 accuracy and robustness requirements. In a two-hour sample window spanning 237 coordination cycles, the protocol surfaces twelve distinct defect classes with zero regressions across a monotonically growing test suite reaching 4,851 passing tests. Eight defects originate in the implementing agent's work and are caught by the verifying agent's independent re-execution. Four originate in the verifying agent's own output and are caught by the same mechanism applied symmetrically. The execution asymmetry between the two agents, one orchestrating multi-phase parallel subagent workflows and the other executing the production chain directly without orchestration, is the structural condition that makes genuine independence possible and that distinguishes this protocol from all prior multi-agent verification approaches. To our knowledge, no prior work demonstrates a dual-agent verification protocol sustaining zero regressions across a session of this duration in a legally consequential production pipeline.
</div></jats:p>
title: Ratification by Re-execution: A Dual-agent Protocol for Independent Verification in Legally Consequential LLM Pipelines

items.abstract: <jats:p>Trace-level characterization is a promising approach for understanding how adversarial influence propagates through resource-operating LLM agents, but current agent-security benchmarks and vulnerability disclosures collapse this propagation into binary outcomes or endpoint categories that obscure where attacks actually stopped. Recent benchmark-audit work has questioned the evidentiary support behind agent-security scores, yet the trace-level propagation structure inside those scores remains uncharacterized. This paper first proposes the Agentic Influence Propagation Framework (AIPF), a trace-level propagation framework with an applicability criterion based on three adversarial objective categories, an exposure marker X, three propagation levels (L1 operational commitment, L2 action materialization, L3 resource realization), and orthogonal episode annotations, and applies it to 180 AgentDojo traces through a three-annotator study spanning senior, junior, and non-specialist expertise. The analysis shows that 4 of 98 benchmark-defended traces reach L3 and 26 of 81 benchmark-successful traces show only shallow propagation, distinctions that the binary outcome collapses. Three case-study groups-a controlled CTF trace, a redacted cloud-agent vulnerability, and four public CVEs-further illustrate the vocabulary's reach beyond benchmark settings. This study provides a structured language for describing where agentic attacks stop and why, and extracts useful distinctions that can inform benchmark design, defence engineering, and agent-specific vulnerability reporting.</jats:p>
title: Beyond Binary Success: Propagation Profiles for LLM Agent Security Traces

This report asks whether that control transfers to language-model agents, and measures the answer. Six

corporate-actions cases built on four real events (a ten-for-one split, an oversubscribed self-tender, two

corrected dividends), eight frontier models from three vendors, and one deterministic grader were run four

account’s position as of any date, a calculator, a test ledger); tools plus a second agent of the same model as

checker, with one revision round; and tools plus one flagship model checking every maker. Tools helped: runs
<br>
that passed every check rose from 32 to 35 of 48, and no run booked on superseded terms. The checker
<br>
lowered the result: 27 of 48 with a same-model reviewer and 25 with the stronger one. The reviewers did the
<br>
tie-out, querying the position in 48 of 48 first rounds and recomputing in 45, and then rejected 20 of the 46
<br>
ledgers the grader scores as correct; every rejection was followed by a revision. Read finding by finding, 13 of
<br>
those 20 rejections and 10 of the stronger reviewer’s 13 raise nothing the documents support. The stronger
<br>
reviewer rejected fewer correct ledgers and found one error the others missed, but told the makers in ten cells
<br>
to replace a correct refusal with a value the documents do not give, and all ten makers complied. Two
<br>
properties of the environment itself induced rejections: a booking tool that requires a payment date no
<br>
document states, and a ledger rendering that reads like an error. The ledgers were never the problem: 46, 44

and 46 of 48 were correct across the three tool arms. The conclusion is narrow and, we think, useful: a checker

needs the maker’s rules, not only the maker’s documents; the environment is part of the control; and makers
<br>

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are beginning to act in banking infrastructure, reconciling payments, triaging fraud alerts and orchestrating back-office workflows. Because a non-deterministic reasoner initiates authenticated, high-value actions, the actor assumptions of existing API security models no longer hold. Building on recent work that moves authorization out of the model and into the execution boundary, we give a formal treatment tailored to regulated banking. An agent is modelled as an untrusted stochastic proposer of typed actions whose authority is a capability set attenuated along a delegation chain, mediated by a deterministic policy engine and single-use, parameter-bounded tokens. We prove (i) authority containment under an arbitrary adversarial proposer, (ii) a closed-form bound on unattended financial loss, (iii) a common-cause analysis of multi-agent review showing that reviewer diversity, not reviewer count, sets the residual-risk floor, with a cost-aware invocation rule, and (iv) soundness of an evidence-only verifier over signed, hash-chained logs, including resistance to log rollback; we also bound the sample size needed to detect policy drift. A reference implementation and simulation with an adversarial proposer (no LLM in the loop) found no unauthorized execution in 700,000 attempts, showed that the loss bound is tight, and exposed two protocol gaps (token expiry and log rollback) that the final design closes. LLM-in-the-loop evaluation and mechanized proofs remain future work.
title: Verifiable Delegated Authority for LLM Agents in Banking: A Formal Architecture, Capability Protocol, and Audit Guarantees

items.abstract: <jats:p>Quick Response (QR) codes are now widely used as a digital communication tool. However, their extensive adoption has made them an attractive target for cyberattacks, particularly through the injection of malicious URLs that redirect users to phishing sites or initiate malware installations. Conventional security approaches such as blacklists and antivirus software are no longer efficient against such evolving threats. This vision paper proposes an AI-based framework using fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify malicious URLs embedded within QR codes. To ensure transparency, a novel ensemble Explainable AI (XAI) is applied to aggregate insights from various XAI methods to explain the features influencing model predictions, facilitating more robust interpretations. To enhance clarity and usability, the proposed framework incorporates personalized explanations tailored to cybersecurity analysts, system developers, and non-expert end users, informed by a role-specific user study. Furthermore, as XAI methods may expose sensitive model behavior, cyberattackers craft adversarial inputs to mislead the model or manipulate explanations. This necessitates the integration of adversarial training to ensure model robustness and explanation integrity, evaluated through perturbation consistency checks. The paper outlines key challenges in explanation fidelity and personalization and presents a development roadmap to advance secure, transparent, and human-centric explainable QR code analysis.</jats:p>
title: A Vision for Robust and Human-Centric LLM-Based QR Code Security

items.abstract: <jats:p>Auto-configuration protocols are used for assignment of unique IP addresses to nodes in Mobile ad hoc networks. Such protocols use various heuristics to ensure the uniqueness in IP address assignment; such aspects increase the overall complexity in MANET system design. Moreover the overriding role of IP address as an ID in Application layer and Locator in routing space is a bottleneck in future wireless network (FWN) design. Our proposed architecture is an adaptation from available ID/Locator split concepts for infrastructure oriented networks for usage in MANET context. The designed protocol uses identifiers for node identification, node discovery and traffic flow between end points. The protocol support provision for running contemporary IP oriented services. items.abstract: <jats:p>Language-model extraction of ESG data is scored against human references that are often revised after the model has run, yet those revisions are seldom versioned or measured. We propose a versioned gold-standard protocol: a blind reference fixed before extraction, every later revision logged with its page evidence and trigger, identical predictions scored against every version, and a worst-case headline. We apply it to 36 stratified Hang Seng Index constituents (396 cells, eleven headline fields). Revisions prompted by model disagreement change 22 cells, 21 toward the model, and raise measured accuracy by 5.1 percentage points with the predictions unchanged. Against the blind reference, a BM25-plus-LLM pipeline scores 90.9% (firm-bootstrap 95% CI 87.1-93.9%) on the 24 firms annotated fully blind and never used in prompt development, and 90.7% on all 36 (89.6% under the pre-specified unit normaliser). A generic regex-and-table heuristic scores 35.6%. Retrieval placed the gold evidence page in the model's context for 98% of disclosed cells, including every missed or wrong value that has a cited page. Under the written prompt, only two of the 37 errors are model errors, plus one masked by an identical gold error. The rest are gold omissions, prompt-gold specification conflicts, definitional ambiguity and unverifiable disclosure. For this reasoning model, residual error arises after retrieval, in the definition of the target; a partial comparison suggests a weaker model loses about ten points. ESG extraction accuracy is a property of a model and a reference together, and benchmarks should report both.</jats:p>
title: Model-Informed Gold Revisions Inflate Measured Accuracy: A Versioned Gold-Standard Protocol for LLM Extraction of ESG Data

items.abstract: <jats:p>The authors develop and validate a systematic methodology for identifying and classifying marketing constructs in text corpora using large language models (LLMs). The Structured Taxonomy AI Measurement Protocol (STAMP) is a standardized, theory-grounded approach that features a multi-layer prompt architecture, a dual-LLM coding process, and a human adjudication process. The method's efficacy is demonstrated across three studies that utilize distinct text-based datasets spanning diverse marketing contexts, including brand communications, product reviews, and sales tactics. The STAMP approach achieves human-level performance (inter-rater reliability: Krippendorff's alpha &gt; .67; and classification accuracy: F1 scores &gt; .80). Compared to extant automated text classification methods such as dictionaries and supervised learning, STAMP offers a transparent, replicable, and scalable solution for analyzing marketing-related content by enhancing classification efficiency and contextual adaptability while maintaining theoretical rigor. This work bridges a critical gap between marketing measurement theory and artificial intelligence capabilities, providing researchers and managers with a standardized framework for analyzing text. A publicly accessible web application that implements the STAMP process accompanies this article (https://tinyurl.com/STAMPTextClassification).</jats:p>
title: STAMP: A Standardized Protocol and Web Application for LLM-based Text Classification

items.abstract: <jats:p>Sensor networks consist of compact sensors and actuators capable of monitoring physical conditions. Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) with limited power and dynamic topology require effective security mechanisms. Insider attacks pose a greater challenge than outsider attacks. This work proposes an Intrusion Detection approach in WSNs to detect attacks, emphasizing experimental results, parameter analysis, and Performance Evaluation based on accuracy and minimizing false positives.</jats:p>
title: ?Implementation of Security Protocol for Intrusion Detection Systems in Wireless Sensor Networks

items.abstract: <jats:p>Current LLM agent security research focuses predominantly on patchable vulnerabilities-prompt injection, jailbreaking, and context manipulation. We demonstrate that psychological attack vectors represent a fundamentally unpatchable vulnerability class because they exploit the cognitive structures necessarily inherited from training on human-generated text. The Cybersecurity Psychology Framework (CPF3) provides the first systematic methodology for identifying, testing, and classifying these architectural vulnerabilities. Through empirical analysis of documented breach cases, we establish that agent failures emerge not from implementation defects but from intrinsic characteristics of language-based reasoning systems. We present the CPF3 Testing Protocol: a rigorous red/blue/purple team methodology for psychological attack surface assessment. We introduce novel metrics including Cognitive Collapse Threshold (CCT) and a comprehensive 28-category failure mode taxonomy spanning seven vulnerability classes. Our findings reveal that all tested agents exhibit finite CCT values, and that security improvements create a Whack-a-Mole pattern where patched vulnerabilities resurface in modified forms. This work does not propose solutions-it establishes a testing framework that illuminates why current architectural approaches cannot resolve the fundamental tension between helpfulness and security in conversational AI systems.</jats:p>
title: The CPF3 Testing Protocol: A Systematic Framework for Assessing Architecturally Unpatchable Psychological Vulnerabilities in LLM Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>In recent years, large language models (LLM) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques have opened up new opportunities for the development of intelligent learning assistant systems. Nevertheless, the direct application of LLMs to Vietnamese Mathematics still has several limitations, including the illusion effect, a lack of knowledge base, failures to adhere to the Vietnamese education curricula, and difficulty in proceessing complex-related image issues. This paper presents the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of a Vietnamese Mathematics Chatbot system based on the RAG architecture combined with LLM. The system comprises: (i) a pineline for collecting and standardizing Mathematics data from textbooks, exam questions and reference materials; (ii) a Milvus vector database to store embeddings generated by the BGE-m3 model; (iii) a multi-task pipeline coordinated by LangGraph; (iv) the inference component uses the Qwen3-VL-8B model implemented via vLLM; and (v) the WebUI user interface supports multimodal queries (text + image). Experimental results show that the system competently delivers detailed solutions, maintains the conversation flow, and significantly mitigates hallucination compared to pure LLM. The system also demonstrates potential for application in teaching and learning Mathematics, especially in situations requiring accurate knowledge retrieval and step-by-step explanations. These results suggest directions towards developing specialized learning assistants within the context of Vietnamese education.</jats:p>
title: BUILDING A VIETNAMESE MATH CHATBOT BASED ON RAG AND LLM: SYSTEM DESIGN, IMPLEMENTATION AND EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION

items.abstract: <jats:p>With the development of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology, multimachine collaborative operations have become the core model for increasing mission effectiveness. However, large-scale UAV clusters face challenges such as dynamic security threats, heterogeneous data fusion difficulties, and resource-constrained decision-making delays. Traditional single-machine intelligent architectures have limitations when addressing new threats, such as insufficient real-time response capabilities. To address these issues, this paper presnts an LLM-layered collaborative security architecture (LLM-LCSA) for multimachine collaborative security. This architecture optimizes the spatiotemporal fusion efficiency of multisource asynchronous data through cloud–edge–end collaborative deployment, combining an end lightweight LLM, an edge medium LLM, and a cloud-based foundation LLM. Additionally, a Mixture of Experts (MoEs) intelligent algorithm that dynamically activates the most relevant expert models by leveraging a threat–expert association matrix is introduced, thereby increasing the accuracy of complex threat identification and dynamic adaptability. Moreover, a resource-aware multi-objective optimization model is constructed to generate optimal decisions under resource constraints. Simulation results indicate that compared with traditional methods, LLM-LCSA achieves an average 7.92% improvement in the threat detection accuracy, reduces the system’s total response time by 44.52%, and enables resource scheduling during off-peak periods. This architecture provides an efficient, intelligent, and scalable solution for secure collaboration among UAV swarms. Future research should further explore its application potential in 6G network integration and large-scale swarm environments.</jats:p>
title: LLM-LCSA: LLM for Collaborative Control and Decision Optimization in UAV Cluster Security

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly combine probabilistic language interpretation with retrieval, persistent memory, external tools, and delegated enterprise credentials. This creates a system-security problem in which untrusted semantic content can cross trust boundaries and acquire operational authority. Existing work provides prompt-injection attacks, agent benchmarks, risk taxonomies, and governance guidance, but less directly addresses how those threats should be translated into verifiable controls for a deployed application. This paper presents a trust-boundary security assurance framework for LLM-integrated and agentic systems. The framework models the application as a mediated-authority system, identifies six architectural threat surfaces and seven recurring trust boundaries, and represents attack paths through source, mechanism, boundary, privilege, asset, and outcome. It then operationalizes the model through a six-stage assurance process covering system decomposition, authority mapping, adversarial scenario construction, boundary-control verification, containment and detection analysis, and evidence-based reporting. A dedicated Model Context Protocol (MCP) profile distinguishes protocol security, semantic trust, and enterprise authorization. The framework further connects defensive controls to observable evidence and proposes a decomposed measurement profile covering attack success, boundary interception, benign-task preservation, blast-radius characteristics, detection latency, and undetected events. A worked enterprise RAG--MCP scenario illustrates how the framework traces an indirect injection from retrieved content through delegated authority to an authorization decision and auditable evidence. The contribution is methodological rather than an empirical claim of defense superiority: it provides a traceable structure for converting evolving LLM and agent threats into testable security claims and application-level assurance evidence.
title: Beyond Prompt Injection: Trust-Boundary Security Assurance for LLM-Integrated and Agentic Applications

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into enterprise and institutional workflows that process sensitive and confidential information including K-12 systems. While security frameworks and guidance documents describe prominent LLM risks and recommended mitigations, K-12 schools still struggle to prioritize controls under real-world constraints. Existing approaches often provide qualitative checklists without a defensible method for selecting mitigations that most effectively reduce high-impact risk.This exploratory research presents an ontology-driven, graph-theoretic framework for prioritizing K-12 LLM security mitigations with a specific focus on confidentiality impact. Using a source LLM security ontology, we construct a multi-layered directed graph linking LLM functions, products, security risks, adversarial techniques, and mitigations. High-confidentiality functions are used as seeds in a function-seeded Personalized PageRank (PPR) analysis to identify attack techniques most structurally exposed to sensitive workflows. To evaluate mitigation effectiveness, we apply eight complementary graph analyses spanning combinatorial optimization, centrality, flow-based separation, stochastic modeling, and community detection.Across analyses, results converge on a small subset of mitigations, most notably AI telemetry logging and generative AI guardrails, as structurally dominant defenses. These controls collectively intercept a disproportionate share of PPR-weighted technique exposure, form low-cost barriers in cut-based analyses, and exhibit high probabilistic interception. Convergence across distinct objectives suggests stable structural bottlenecks rather than artifacts of graph size or algorithm choice. By integrating semantic richness from security ontologies with established attack-graph analytics, the exploratory research provides an approach for selecting high-impact mitigations in confidentiality-sensitive K-12 LLM deployments.
title: Ontology-Driven Graph Framework for Prioritizing K-12 LLM Security Mitigations
